mainTopic: Whether יאוש שלא מדעת (unknowing despair) counts: the thief, river and תרומה sources, and the orchard story
overview: The גמרא is testing whether יאוש שלא מדעת counts as real יאוש. That means an owner who would give up hope, but does not yet know his item is gone. First it finishes a ברייתא saying that what a גנב, a גזלן or the ירדן river takes stays taken. It challenges אביי from the thief case, but רב פפא explains that the 'thief' is an armed bandit whom the owner sees. Next, a ברייתא about a river sweeping beams into another's field seems to prove unknowing despair does not count. The גמרא explains that the owners could rescue the items only with difficulty, so their chasing or not chasing shows their attitude. Then a ברייתא about separating תרומה from someone else's produce seems to show that approval nobody knew about still counts. רבא answers for אביי that the person was already the owner's שליח, as the פסוק 'גם אתם' requires. A story with מר זוטרא in the orchard of מרי בר איסק teaches that 'go to the nicer ones' shows real approval only for a מצוה like תרומה, not when an owner speaks out of embarrassment. The amud ends by starting a new proof about dew on produce and the owner's happiness, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: End of the ברייתא: what the river takes and gives stays put
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא being quoted ends by saying that when the ירדן river carries something from one person's land to another's, the result stands.
steps.simpleTranslation: And likewise the ירדן river that took from this one and gave to that one: what it took, it took, and what it gave, it gave.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing a ברייתא it began quoting just before this point. The last case is a river moving property from one owner to another, and the ruling is that the new holder keeps it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא lumps the ירדן together with a גנב and a גזלן. In all of these cases, the item now belongs to whoever ended up with it. The reason, as the next step assumes, is that the original owner has given up hope.

keyTerms.meaning: The Jordan river, used here as the classic example of a river that carries things away
Took from this one and gave to that one

keyTerms.term: מַה שֶּׁנָּטַל נָטַל וּמַה שֶּׁנָּתַן נָתַן
keyTerms.meaning: What was taken stays taken, and what was given stays given; the change of ownership stands

phrases.english: And likewise the Jordan that took
from this one and gave to that one,
what it took, it took,
and what it gave, it gave.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכֵן יַרְדֵּן שֶׁנָּטַל מִזֶּה וְנָתַן לָזֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes a ברייתא quoted before this point in the daf
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Items moved by the ירדן, a גנב, or a גזלן stay with whoever now holds them, because the owner has given up hope.

steps.title: How can there be giving up hope in a thief case?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא accepts יאוש for a גזלן and a river, since the owner sees them happen. It asks how a גנב case works, since a thief takes things secretly.
steps.simpleTranslation: It makes sense for a robber and the Jordan, since the owner sees them and gives up hope. But a thief: does the owner see him, so that he would give up hope?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא uses the ברייתא's גנב case to challenge אביי. A thief works in secret, so the owner does not know of the loss, yet the ברייתא says the taker keeps it, as if unknowing despair counts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A גזלן robs openly and a flood is visible to everyone, so the owner knows right away and despairs. A גנב sneaks the item away, so at the moment of the theft the owner does not know. Why, then, does the ברייתא treat the thief like the others?

keyTerms.meaning: It makes sense for this case (but not for another)
A robber who takes openly, by force
A thief who takes secretly
Gives up hope of getting the item back (יֵאוּשׁ)

phrases.english: It makes sense for a robber and the Jordan,
since he sees them and gives up hope.
But a thief,
does he see him, so that he gives up hope?

steps.triggerLanguage: בִּשְׁלָמָא גַּזְלָן וְיַרְדֵּן דְּקָא חָזֵי לְהוּ וּמִיָּאַשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions one of the cases in the ברייתא just quoted
steps.kashyaTarget: אביי's view that יאוש שלא מדעת is not יאוש, challenged from the ברייתא's גנב case
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: With a גזלן or a river the owner sees the loss, so his despair is known. A secret גנב leaves the owner unaware, yet the ברייתא still says the taker keeps the item. That looks like יאוש שלא מדעת counting, against אביי.

steps.title: רב פפא: the thief is an armed bandit
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא explains that the 'thief' in the ברייתא is an armed bandit, whom the owner does see.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא explained it as referring to an armed bandit.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא answers by redefining the גנב in the ברייתא as a ליסטים מזוין, an armed bandit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An armed bandit does not hide; the owner sees him and is too afraid to resist. So the owner knows about the loss and gives up hope, just like in the robber case.

keyTerms.meaning: He explained it (interpreted the source)
An armed bandit

phrases.english: Rav Pappa explained it
as an armed bandit.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about the גנב
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The גנב is an ordinary secret thief, whom the owner never sees
steps.terutzMaskana: The 'thief' is an armed bandit whom the owner sees, so the owner does give up hope

steps.title: Then the bandit is just a robber
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that an armed bandit is the same as a גזלן, which the ברייתא already listed.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, that is the same as a robber!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב פפא's answer. If the 'thief' is an armed bandit, he is no different from the robber the ברייתא already mentioned.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A ברייתא should not list the same case twice. If the bandit and the גזלן are both open takers, the ברייתא seems to repeat itself.

keyTerms.meaning: If so (if your answer is true)
That is the same as

phrases.english: If so, that is the same as a robber!

steps.kashyaTarget: רב פפא's explanation that the thief is an armed bandit
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: An armed bandit is just another robber, so the ברייתא would be listing the same case twice

steps.title: Two kinds of robbers
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the ברייתא lists two different types of גזלן.
steps.simpleTranslation: There are two kinds of robber.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the ברייתא is not repeating itself. It is naming two types of open robber.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both the 'גנב' (armed bandit) and the 'גזלן' are seen by the owner, so both lead to יאוש. The ברייתא simply mentions both kinds, and this closes the question.

keyTerms.meaning: Two kinds, two types

steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא's thief, robber and river cases all involve an owner who knows about his loss. That is why the taker keeps the item.

phrases.english: Two kinds of robber.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the objection that the ברייתא repeats itself
steps.terutzResolutionType: Showing the two cases are distinct sub-types
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא lists the same case twice
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא lists two types of robbers, both of whom the owner sees

steps.title: Proof from the river that swept away beams
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says swept-away items belong to the field owner 'because the owners despaired.' The גמרא infers that without known despair, the field owner would not keep them.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come hear: If a river swept away someone's beams, wood and stones and put them in his friend's field, they belong to the field owner, because the owners despaired. The reason is that the owners despaired; but in an unclear case, no!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new source and draws a precise inference from its wording. This is an attempt to prove that יאוש שלא מדעת (unknowing despair) does not count.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא gives a reason: 'because the owners despaired.' That suggests the finder keeps the items only when we know the owners despaired. In an unclear case, where we only assume they would despair, the items are not his, so unknowing despair is not real despair.

keyTerms.meaning: A river swept away
These belong to him (the finder)
The reason is (used to make an inference from the wording)
An unclear case, where the owner's attitude is not known
Giving up hope without yet knowing the item is lost

steps.confusionAlert: The inference comes from the words 'because the owners despaired,' not from the river itself. The גמרא reads those words as excluding a case where we are not sure the owners gave up.

phrases.english: Come hear:
If a river swept away his beams, his wood, and his stones,
and placed them in his friend's field,
these are his,
phrases.notes: 'His' means they belong to the owner of the field where they landed.

phrases.english: because the owners gave up hope.
The reason is that the owners gave up hope,
but in an unclear case, no!

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: שָׁטַף נָהָר קוֹרָיו, עֵצָיו, וַאֲבָנָיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a new source into the larger question of יאוש שלא מדעת
steps.raayaObject: That יאוש שלא מדעת does not count as יאוש
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא's stated reason, 'because the owners gave up hope,' implies that an unclear case does not work
steps.whyThisMatters: This is a direct test of whether unknowing despair counts. That question decides when a finder may keep a lost item.

steps.title: The owners were able to rescue the items
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof. The ברייתא is about owners who could have saved their things, so their not doing so shows clear despair.
steps.simpleTranslation: What case are we dealing with here? When he is able to rescue them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes away the proof by placing the ברייתא in a specific case: the owners could have saved their beams and stones.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the owners could have saved the items and did not bother, they have openly given up. So the words 'because the owners despaired' fit this case. The ברייתא says nothing about an unclear case of unknowing despair.

keyTerms.meaning: What case are we dealing with here? (used to narrow a source to a specific case)
Able to rescue

phrases.english: With what are we dealing here?
When he is able to rescue them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof brought in the previous step
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the inference from the ברייתא's wording
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ברייתא is about owners who could have saved their things and chose not to, which is clear despair. It does not speak about an unclear case.

steps.title: The סיפא doesn't fit 'able to rescue'
steps.stepSummary: The סיפא says the finder must return the items if the owners chase after them. If the owners could rescue the items, why does the ברייתא need them to be chasing?
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, say the last part: If the owners were chasing after them, he must return them. If they are able to rescue, why mention chasing? Even if they are not chasing, they should get them back too!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the answer of 'able to rescue' using the last part of the same ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the items can easily be saved, the owners would not give up even without chasing. Then the ברייתא's condition, 'if the owners were chasing,' would be pointless. So 'able to rescue' does not seem to fit the ברייתא.

keyTerms.meaning: The last part of a משנה or ברייתא
Chasing after (the items)
Obligated to return
Why specifically this? (why mention this detail)

phrases.english: If so, say the last part:
If the owners were chasing after them,
he must return them.
If they are able to rescue,
why specifically chasing?
Even if they are not chasing, also!
phrases.notes: He means: even without chasing, the finder should still have to give the items back.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer given in the previous step
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that the ברייתא is about owners who are able to rescue
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If rescue is possible, the owners never give up, so the סיפא's condition of chasing would be unnecessary

steps.title: Able to rescue, but only with difficulty
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא refines its answer: the owners can rescue the items only with effort. Chasing shows they have not given up; not chasing shows they have.
steps.simpleTranslation: What case are we dealing with here? When they are able to rescue only with difficulty. If they chase, they have not given up hope; if they don't chase, they have certainly given up hope.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by making the case more specific. Saving the items is possible, but hard.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since rescue is hard, the owners' behavior tells us what they are thinking. Chasing means they still hope, so the finder must return the items. Not chasing means they have clearly given up. Either way, the ברייתא speaks about known despair, so it still does not prove anything about unknowing despair.

keyTerms.meaning: With difficulty, with great effort
He has certainly given up hope

steps.whatToRemember: The river ברייתא is about owners who can save their things only with difficulty. Whether they chase shows whether they gave up, so the ברייתא is about known despair. It cannot prove that unknowing despair fails to count.

phrases.english: With what are we dealing here?
When they are able to rescue with difficulty.
If they chase, they have not given up hope,
if they don't chase, they have certainly given up hope.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָכָא בְּמַאי עָסְקִינַן בִּיכוֹלִין לְהַצִּיל עַל יְדֵי הַדְּחָק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from the סיפא by refining the answer of 'able to rescue'
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Able to rescue' means easily, which would make the chasing condition pointless
steps.terutzMaskana: It means able to rescue only with difficulty, so chasing or not chasing shows whether the owners gave up
steps.whyThisMatters: This keeps the river ברייתא from deciding the question of יאוש שלא מדעת, so the larger debate stays open.

steps.title: A ברייתא about separating תרומה from someone else's field
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא: someone who separates תרומה from another person's produce without permission. If the owner sees it as robbery, it is not תרומה. If he does not mind, it is תרומה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: When did the חכמים say that one who separates תרומה without the owner's knowledge, his תרומה counts? Where someone went into his friend's field, gathered produce, and separated תרומה without permission. If the owner is upset and sees it as robbery, his תרומה is not תרומה. If not, his תרומה is תרומה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new proof by quoting a ברייתא. Here it only sets up the source; the actual argument comes a few lines later, in step 12.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא says the תרומה works or fails depending on how the owner feels about it. That sounds like the owner's attitude can count even when he has not said anything yet. This will become the basis for a challenge to אביי's view on יאוש שלא מדעת.

keyTerms.meaning: The portion of produce given to a כהן
One who separates תרומה without the owner knowing
Without permission
Upset about it, seeing it as robbery

phrases.english: Come and hear:
When did they say
that one who separates teruma without the owner's knowledge
his teruma is teruma?
Where someone went down into his friend's field
and gathered and separated teruma without permission.
If he is bothered by it as robbery,
phrases.notes: The one who is bothered is the field's owner, not the person who took the produce.

phrases.english: his teruma is not teruma,
and if not, his teruma is teruma.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: כֵּיצַד אָמְרוּ הַתּוֹרֵם שֶׁלֹּא מִדַּעַת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the earlier proof was pushed aside in step 9, the גמרא brings a new source on the same question.
steps.raayaObject: Whether an owner's attitude that is not yet known still counts, which bears on יאוש שלא מדעת

steps.title: How we know whether the owner minds
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא explains how we find out the owner's attitude. If he says 'go take the nicer ones' and nicer produce really exists, the תרומה counts. If the owners themselves add to it, it counts no matter what.
steps.simpleTranslation: And how does he know whether the owner sees it as robbery or not? If the owner came, found him, and said: 'You should have gone to the nice ones.' If nicer produce than this is found, his תרומה is תרומה. If not, it is not תרומה. If the owners gathered and added to it, either way his תרומה is תרומה.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues and asks itself how we can tell what the owner feels. It answers with tests based on what the owner says or does afterward.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Go to the nice ones' could be sincere or sarcastic. If nicer produce really exists, we take him at his word and assume he is pleased. If not, he was probably mocking. If the owners actively add more produce, they clearly agree. In every test, the owner's approval shows up only after the separating was already done.

keyTerms.meaning: The owner
Go over to the nicer ones
Either way

phrases.english: And how does he know

phrases.aramaic: אִם חוֹשֵׁשׁ מִשּׁוּם גָּזֵל וְאִם לָאו?
phrases.english: whether the owner is bothered by it as robbery or not?
Where the owner came and found him,
and said to him: 'Go over to the nice ones.'
If nicer ones than these are found,
his teruma is teruma,
and if not, his teruma is not teruma.
If the owners gathered and added to them,

phrases.aramaic: בֵּין כָּךְ וּבֵין כָּךְ – תְּרוּמָתוֹ תְּרוּמָה.
phrases.english: either way, his teruma is teruma.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִנַּיִן הוּא יוֹדֵעַ אִם חוֹשֵׁשׁ מִשּׁוּם גָּזֵל וְאִם לָאו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא and explains how to test the owner's attitude.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How do we know whether the owner minds or not?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: By his later reaction: a sincere 'go to the nicer ones', or the owners adding to the תרומה.

steps.title: The approval came after the separating
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the תרומה counts when nicer produce is found. At the moment he separated, he did not yet know the owner would approve.
steps.simpleTranslation: But when nicer produce is found and his תרומה is תרומה, why? At the time he separated, he did not know the owner agreed!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now makes its point from the ברייתא. Approval that nobody knew about at the time still made the תרומה valid.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This works just like יאוש שלא מדעת: something that was true but not yet known still counts. If unknown approval works for תרומה, then unknown despair should work for lost objects. That goes against אביי.

keyTerms.meaning: Why?
At the time
Despair the owner is not yet aware of; the topic of the whole סוגיא

steps.confusionAlert: Although it is worded as a question on the ברייתא, its real job is to prove something against אביי from the ברייתא.

phrases.english: But when nicer ones than these are found
and his teruma is teruma — why?
At the time that he separated,
he did not know!
phrases.notes: He did not yet know the owner would be happy. That only came out afterward.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי נִמְצְאוּ יָפוֹת מֵהֶן תְּרוּמָתוֹ תְּרוּמָה, אַמַּאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the challenge out of the ברייתא quoted in steps 10-11.
steps.raayaObject: Unknown approval or despair still counts, against אביי
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא's ruling that the תרומה is valid once nicer produce is found
steps.kashyaTarget: אביי's view that יאוש שלא מדעת is not יאוש
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The owner's approval was not known when the person separated, yet it still makes the תרומה count.

steps.title: רבא: the owner had made him a שליח
steps.stepSummary: רבא explains the ברייתא in a way that fits אביי: the owner had already appointed this person as his שליח.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא explained the ברייתא according to אביי: the case is where the owner made him his שליח.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא pushes the proof aside. The ברייתא is not about unknown approval at all, because the person was already appointed as the owner's שליח.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If he was already a שליח, he separated with the owner's permission from the start. The only open question was whether the owner was fine with his using the better produce, and the owner's remark answers that. So the case teaches nothing about יאוש שלא מדעת.

keyTerms.meaning: He explained it
According to the view of
An agent who acts for someone else

phrases.english: Rava explained it according to Abaye:
that he made him an agent.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof from step 12 by changing how we picture the case.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The whole proof from the ברייתא
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed there was no permission at the time. In fact he was already the owner's שליח.

steps.title: It must be a שליח, because of the פסוק
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא shows רבא's reading is the only sensible one. The Torah teaches that a שליח can separate תרומה only with the owner's knowledge, so without being appointed it would not work at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: So too it is logical. If you thought he was not appointed a שליח, would his תרומה be תרומה? The Torah said 'you' and 'you also' to include your שליח. Just as you separate with your own knowledge, so too your שליח must separate with your knowledge.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא backs up רבא's answer. Without being made a שליח, the person's separating could never have worked.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'גם אתם' include a שליח and compare him to the owner. Just as the owner separates knowingly, a שליח must act with the owner's knowledge. So the ברייתא must be about an appointed שליח, and the proof against אביי falls away.

keyTerms.meaning: So too it is logical; a phrase supporting the answer just given
It would enter your mind
The Torah, literally 'the Merciful One'
To include

steps.whatToRemember: The תרומה ברייתא does not prove יאוש שלא מדעת. It works only because the person was already a שליח, and a שליח must act with the owner's knowledge. אביי's view survives this challenge.
steps.whyThisMatters: It establishes that someone can separate תרומה for another person only as his appointed שליח, never on his own.

phrases.english: So too it is logical,
for if it would enter your mind
that he did not make him an agent,
would his teruma be teruma?
But the Torah said 'you,' 'you also'
phrases.notes: במדבר 18:28. The extra word 'גם' (also) is what adds the שליח.

phrases.english: to include your agent.
Just as you separate with your own knowledge,
so too your agent must separate with your knowledge.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רבא's answer in step 13 with a פסוק.
steps.raayaObject: רבא's reading that the ברייתא is about an appointed שליח
steps.raayaSupportSource: במדבר 18:28, 'גם אתם', which includes a שליח acting with the owner's knowledge

steps.title: Defining the exact case: the owner appointed a שליח but did not say which produce
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא is about a person the owner did appoint as a שליח, but without saying which produce to use. The שליח took from the nicer produce instead of the usual medium produce. The owner's reaction decides whether it counts.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, what case is this? The owner made him a שליח and said 'Go separate תרומה,' but did not say 'from these.' Normally an owner separates from medium-quality produce. This שליח went and separated from the nicer produce. The owner came, found him, and said: 'You should have gone to the even nicer ones!' If nicer produce than what he took really exists, his תרומה counts. If not, it does not count.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now spells out the full case behind the ברייתא, following רבא's reading that the person was already a שליח. The question is only about which produce he took.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The שליח was sent, but an unspecified mission means medium-quality produce, and he took better produce, so he went beyond his orders. If even nicer produce exists, the owner's words 'go to the nicer ones' are real, so he clearly approves. If no nicer produce exists, his words cannot be meant literally, so they show no approval and the שליח simply went beyond his job.

keyTerms.meaning: "What case are we dealing with here?" The גמרא's phrase for narrowing a source to a specific case.
He appointed him as an agent.
Medium-quality produce, the normal default for separating תרומה.
"Go over to the nicer ones": the owner's reaction that can show approval.

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the 'nicer produce' test is about the quality of the תרומה itself. It is only a way to check whether the owner's words were real approval or not.

phrases.english: Rather, with what case are we dealing here?
For example, where he appointed him as an agent,
and said to him: "Go separate תרומה,"
but did not say to him: "Separate from these."
And the usual way of a homeowner,
when he separates, is to separate from medium-quality produce,
phrases.notes: Some versions leave out the word in round brackets. The meaning stays the same.

phrases.english: and he (the agent) went and separated from the nice produce,
and the owner came and found him
and said to him: "Go over to the nicer ones,"
if nicer ones than these are found,
his תרומה is תרומה,
and if not, his תרומה is not תרומה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes רבא's reading from steps 13–14 by giving the full case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא seemed to be about a stranger with no permission, whose action is approved only afterward.
steps.terutzMaskana: He was a שליח from the start. The only issue is whether taking nicer produce matches the owner's wishes, and that is shown by his reaction.

steps.title: The story of the sages in the orchard of מרי בר איסק
steps.stepSummary: A sharecropper serves fruit to three sages. Two of them eat but מר זוטרא does not. The owner arrives and asks why the sharecropper did not bring them the nicer fruit.
steps.simpleTranslation: אמימר, מר זוטרא and רב אשי came to the orchard of מרי בר איסק. His sharecropper brought dates and pomegranates and set them before them. אמימר and רב אשי ate, but מר זוטרא did not. Meanwhile מרי בר איסק arrived, found them, and said to his sharecropper: 'Why didn't you bring the רבנן some of those nicer ones?'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a real-life story that matches the ברייתא's 'go to the nicer ones' case. It is setting up a question about מר זוטרא in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The sharecropper gave away fruit that belonged to the owner, without asking him. מר זוטרא held back, probably worried the owner did not approve. The owner's words sound just like 'כְּלָךְ אֵצֶל יָפוֹת', which is the comparison the next step will use.

keyTerms.meaning: An orchard.
A sharecropper, a worker who farms the owner's field for a share of the crop.
Nice, high-quality ones.

phrases.english: Ameimar, Mar Zutra, and Rav Ashi
happened to come to the orchard of Mari bar Isak.
His sharecropper brought dates and pomegranates
and put them before them.
Ameimar and Rav Ashi ate;
Mar Zutra did not eat.
Meanwhile, Mari bar Isak came,
found them, and said to his sharecropper:
"Why didn't you bring the Rabbis
some of those nice ones?"

steps.triggerLanguage: אַמֵּימָר וּמָר זוּטְרָא וְרַב אָשֵׁי אִקְּלַעוּ לְבוּסְתָּנָא דְּמָרִי בַּר אִיסַק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A real-life story that parallels the 'go to the nicer ones' case just defined.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Two sages ate fruit from the sharecropper and מר זוטרא held back. The owner then said: 'Why not the nicer ones?'

steps.title: Why won't מר זוטרא eat now?
steps.stepSummary: אמימר and רב אשי challenge מר זוטרא from the ברייתא. The owner's words 'bring the nicer ones' should prove he approves.
steps.simpleTranslation: אמימר and רב אשי said to מר זוטרא: 'Now, why doesn't the master eat? Didn't we learn: if nicer ones are found, his תרומה counts?'
steps.whatsHappening: The two sages use the ברייתא to challenge מר זוטרא. Now that the owner has spoken, they say his approval is clear.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the ברייתא, 'go to the nicer ones' plus the real existence of nicer produce proves the owner approves. Here the owner said the same thing and nicer fruit exists, so the fruit should be allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: Now, meaning after the owner has shown his attitude.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ אַמֵּימָר וְרַב אָשֵׁי לְמָר זוּטְרָא:
phrases.english: Ameimar and Rav Ashi said to Mar Zutra:
"Now, why doesn't the master eat?
But it was taught:

phrases.aramaic: אִם נִמְצְאוּ יָפוֹת מֵהֶן – תְּרוּמָתוֹ תְּרוּמָה!
phrases.english: If nicer ones than these are found, his תרומה is תרומה!"
phrases.notes: This is the ברייתא quoted in step 11.

steps.triggerLanguage: הַשְׁתָּא אַמַּאי לָא אָכֵיל מָר? וְהָתַנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the ברייתא to the story and challenges מר זוטרא's choice.
steps.kashyaTarget: מר זוטרא's refusal to eat after the owner spoke.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The owner's words match 'כְּלָךְ אֵצֶל יָפוֹת', which the ברייתא treats as proof of approval.

steps.title: The rule only works for תרומה, because it is a מצוה
steps.stepSummary: מר זוטרא answers in the name of רבא. 'Go to the nicer ones' shows real approval only for תרומה, which the owner is glad to see done. With the fruit, the owner spoke only out of embarrassment.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: this is what רבא said. 'Go to the nicer ones' was only said about תרומה, because it is a מצוה and the owner is happy with it. But here, he said it only out of embarrassment.
steps.whatsHappening: מר זוטרא defends himself. The ברייתא's proof of approval does not carry over to giving away fruit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With תרומה, the owner gains a מצוה, so his words are believed as real happiness. With fruit given to guests, he loses money. His polite words may just be him saving face in front of the Rabbis, so they do not prove he truly agrees.

keyTerms.meaning: A commandment. Separating תרומה is something the owner is glad to have done.
He is pleased with it, so it is his real wish.
Embarrassment, shame.

steps.whatToRemember: The same words ('bring the nicer ones') can show real approval or just politeness, depending on whether the owner gains (a מצוה) or loses (his fruit).
steps.whyThisMatters: It teaches that a person's words are judged in context. Polite words said out of embarrassment are not true consent to take his property.

phrases.english: He said to them: This is what Rava said:
They said "go over to the nicer ones" counts
only with regard to תרומה,
because it is a מצוה and he is pleased with it;
but here,
it was out of embarrassment that he said this.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לְהוּ, הָכִי אָמַר רָבָא: לֹא אָמְרוּ כְּלָךְ אֵצֶל יָפוֹת אֶלָּא לְעִנְיַן תְּרוּמָה בִּלְבַד
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The owner's words always prove approval, so the fruit is allowed.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only for תרומה, a מצוה the owner wants. For his fruit, polite words may come from embarrassment and prove nothing.

steps.title: New proof: dew on produce and the owner's happiness
steps.stepSummary: A new ברייתא about produce that dew fell on. If the owner is happy while the dew is still on it, the produce becomes able to receive טומאה (כי יותן). If he is happy only after it dried, a different ruling follows, which is finished in the next part.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: if the dew is still on the produce and the owner is happy about it, it falls under 'כי יותן'. If it already dried, even though he was happy...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new proof from a ברייתא about dew. It is setting up a point that is finished in the next part of the text.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Produce can receive טומאה only after it gets wet in a way the owner wants (כי יותן). The ברייתא contrasts being happy while it is still wet with being happy only after it dried. This tests whether a later attitude can count for something that already happened.

keyTerms.meaning: Dew, one of the liquids that can make produce able to receive טומאה.
"When water is put" (ויקרא 11:38): produce that got wet in a way the owner wants becomes able to receive טומאה.
They dried off.

phrases.english: Come and hear: If the dew is still on them
and he was happy, this falls under "when water is put."
If they dried, even though he was happy...

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: עוֹדֵהוּ הַטַּל עֲלֵיהֶן וְשָׂמַח
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the story, the גמרא goes back to bringing sources on whether a later attitude counts, now from the laws of טומאה.
steps.raayaObject: Whether an owner's attitude formed afterward can work back on something that already happened.
steps.raayaSupportSource: ברייתא about dew on produce and כי יותן.
